remarks: This is an FGD-only record (Mode B); no official ED interview exists for Consent to Establish in Maharashtra in the current dataset, so these structured fields are derived from business-participant testimony and have not been verified against an official source.
Participants viewed Consent to Establish as substantially overlapping with Consent to Operate renewal and suggested removing it or converting it to self-certification.

findings.text: Applications are rejected without any written communication of the grounds of rejection, leaving applicants unable to identify what needs to be corrected.
Department queries are often valid in substance but are not communicated properly, making them difficult to respond to.
No facility exists to track the stage-wise progress of an application online, prolonging the process and requiring repeated follow-up with the department.
The system issues only a single message to the applicant; if that message is missed, no further message is sent and the application remains pending unnoticed.
Compliance equipment costs between fifteen and twenty lakh rupees, machines must be procured from a particular vendor, and the deposit demanded is at the higher end.
An applicant proceeding without assistance takes four to five months, whereas the same application through a consultant takes about two months, effectively making consultant engagement necessary.
Applications falling in the red and orange categories are referred to Mumbai rather than decided locally, adding time and travel to the process.
Participants questioned why a Consent to Establish is required where the unit is already renewing its Consent to Operate, and why the CTE fee is charged after the CTO has been granted.
Categorisation is not aligned to actual pollution load; a unit generating no hazardous waste was nonetheless placed in the red and then orange category.
The category is changed at the time of recertification even where there has been no change in the nature of the unit's activity.
The rate charged is the same across cities and, in participants' view, ought to vary according to the location of the unit.
The bank guarantee is fixed in proportion to the investment made; participants saw no need for such a requirement.
Documentation has nominally been narrowed to five prescribed documents, but approximately twenty-five underlying documents are required to produce those five.
Applicants are required to fetch new documents on every occasion instead of relying on documents already held by the department.
The location recorded on Google Earth does not match the GPS location of the site, and mismatched geolocation data between departments gives rise to objections during scrutiny.
Participants questioned the necessity of submitting a project report and stated that a chartered accountant certificate should not be required for this service.
Consent to Establish was described as duplicative where the unit already holds and is renewing a Consent to Operate, since the same particulars are examined afresh.
Participants suggested removing the Consent to Establish requirement altogether, or replacing it with self-certification by the applicant.
Participants suggested enabling online tracking of application status and issuing a repeat message where the first message is not acted upon.
The approval is granted online, which participants acknowledged as an improvement, though they stated the absence of tracking limits its usefulness.

remarks: This is an FGD-only record (Mode B); no official ED interview exists for Consent to Operate in Maharashtra in the current dataset.
Green and white category units were stated to be subject to lighter requirements than red category units.
Distilleries additionally require a licence from the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation.

findings.text: A Consent to Operate in the red category takes approximately four months; participants described the process as lengthy and in need of being made time-bound.
Applications of units with a project value above ten crore rupees are dealt with at Mumbai rather than Kolhapur, requiring applicants to travel.
No facility exists to track the status of an application, so applicants remain unaware of the stage at which it rests.
Where an error is identified during scrutiny, the applicant is required to visit the office in person to have it rectified.
The documentation process is difficult and alone takes ten to fifteen days, so applicants engage consultants to complete it.
Participants reported facing harassment at the management level and identified bribery as an issue in the course of the approval process.
The first interaction with the officer takes place only at the query stage, which participants identified as a source of difficulty.
Different guidelines are issued from time to time and differ from one another, making it difficult to know which requirement applies.
A penalty is levied where renewal is not applied for within 120 days, and a penalty also applies even where the delay in the Consent to Operate itself is attributable to the department.
Charges are collected before expiry of the current consent and described as high; charges are also levied for the gap period where a company restarts after a period of closure.
Jurisdiction is determined by project value — applications under ten crore rupees are decided at Kolhapur and above that at Mumbai — adding to the burden on larger units.

Renewal must be applied for within 120 days; third-party inspection is required for certain stack reports; combined/random inspections occur in some instances; distilleries require an additional PESO licence; a chartered accountant certificate must be furnished.
Details already held by the department must be furnished afresh, as no facility for automatic fetching of particulars exists.
The chartered accountant certificate was identified as a requirement participants considered unnecessary for the purposes of this service.
Participants suggested that where a unit continues the same activity, the consent should continue automatically instead of the entire process being repeated.
Participants suggested introducing a tracking facility and auto-fetch of particulars already held by the department.
Participants asked that the process be made time-bound, with a definite timeline prescribed and adhered to.
Participants asked that the penalty and charging structure be reviewed, including the penalty for departmental delay, pre-expiry charging, and gap-period charging.

findings.text: The LMS portal on which the application is filed is not user-friendly and goes down during the night, interrupting work.
There is no auto-fetch facility, so the same documents are uploaded again at each annual application although they are unchanged and already held on the portal.
Documents must be compressed before upload due to file size limits, deteriorating file quality and requiring repeated re-upload when queries are raised.
Queries are raised roughly fifteen days after the application is filed, with four to six queries on average before the matter is settled.
The period from submission to grant runs to about forty to fifty days, with a provisional licence issued in the interim.
Compliance requirements are communicated orally by the inspecting officer and not given in writing, leaving the applicant with no record of what was asked for.
The fee already paid is retained on rejection, and where the premises change within the validity period a fresh licence must be taken with the full fee paid again.
Grievances can be lodged via the helpline, but no reply follows either on the portal or by email.
The fee structure should be reviewed, per participants.
MAITRI and MAITRI 2.0 have not resolved earlier difficulties; LMS documentation still requires manual effort through physical visits.
Documents already held by other departments, particularly the Consent to Operate granted by the Pollution Control Board, are demanded again for this service.
The safety audit report and HIRA must be obtained from an empanelled third-party auditor and add separately to the cost of the application.
Participants asked that the LMS portal be made stable and redesigned around how an applicant uses it, with downtime (particularly at night) addressed.
Participants asked for auto-fetch of already-filed documents, with only new or changed material required at the annual application.
Participants asked that inspection observations and required compliances be given in writing so a record exists and the same ground is not revisited.
Participants asked that grievances lodged through the helpline, portal and email receive a reply.

The expiry period prescribed for fire extinguishers should be increased, from one year to at least three years.
